title: Neighbor bitlines form a SAR DAC for two-bit cells
idea: Ideal result: the bitline itself is the analog-to-digital converter. Store 4 charge levels per cell and resolve them by successive approximation, with adjacent precharged bitlines switched in binary-weighted groups acting as the DAC capacitors against the sensed line.
why: Density and cost per bit: 2 bits/cell at ~1.3x periphery cost gives ~1.5x bits per wafer without a litho shrink (fact 4).

title: Pulsed segmented cell plate borrowed from FeRAM boosts signal
idea: Split DRAM's common VDD/2 plate into row-wise segments and pulse the selected row's plate by +0.5 V during charge sharing (the FeRAM plate-line drive), so the stored node is coupled upward and the differential bitline signal grows; the plate returns to VDD/2 before restore.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and voltage floor (fact 10): ~1.5-2x bitline signal at the same Cs, allowing 30-40% lower Cs or longer bitlines (fewer SA stripes, fact 7).

title: Frequency-tuned resonators select mats instead of decoder wiring
idea: Shift the address from space to frequency: each mat's local wordline-driver enable is gated by a micron-scale AlN film-bulk acoustic resonator tuned to a unique GHz tone, and one shared RF line selects a mat by broadcasting its tone; only a short local decoder picks the row inside the mat. Predecoders and the global address bus collapse into one line plus a frequency synthesizer.
why: Attacks decoder and global-routing periphery (fact 7) and address-bus wire energy; est. 3-6% die area saved and fewer routing metal layers.

title: Wavelength-addressed photoconductive switches replace electrical row decoders
idea: Effect: photoconductivity. Run a BEOL SiN waveguide past each sub-wordline driver group, where a ring filter tuned to one of ~64 WDM wavelengths feeds a Ge or a-Si photoconductor that gates the driver; the controller picks a row block by injecting that wavelength, so address decoding happens in the waveguide instead of in CMOS decoder trees.
why: Periphery area/energy (fact 7): removes predecoders and global address wires; photoconductive turn-on is <100 ps.

title: Zero-leakage idle sensing: pre-biased NEMS cantilever latch
idea: Limit: idle sense amps must leak exactly zero. Each SA is a nano-electromechanical relay biased within ~30 mV of pull-in, so the bitline differential tips the beam toward the BL or BLB electrode; once in contact it latches mechanically, then releases on reset.
why: Idle power and refresh energy (fact 3) plus periphery leakage: zero off-current and an abrupt switch. Risk: contact wear over 1e15 cycles and ~ns mechanical delay.

title: ThruChip inductive links tucked under the sense-amp stripe
idea: Failure mined: Keio's ThruChip inductive coupling and Samsung's Wide I/O both died, coils on area cost and TSVs on yield cost. Fix: lay the coupling coils in spare top metal directly over sense-amp stripes and arrays, beat crosstalk with code-division multiplexing among neighboring coils, and receive with sense-amp-style clocked latches. Data then crosses 8-12 thinned dies with no signal TSVs, only power vias.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removing signal TSVs and their keep-out zones recovers part of the ~3x area-per-bit penalty and the 20-30% yield loss, because failed dies can be swapped before final bonding.

title: 16-level DRAM via segmented-bitline capacitive-DAC successive approximation
idea: Failure mined: the 1990s multi-level DRAMs from Toshiba and NEC died because splitting ~150 mV into many levels destroyed margin and their staircase sensing was slow. Fix: split each bitline into binary-weighted segments that double as the capacitor DAC of a 4-step successive-approximation sense, trimmed per subarray against a stored reference charge, with one SAR comparator shared by 4 bitlines.
why: 10x at the same cost: 4 bits per cell in an open-bitline 4F^2 cell (6x vs 1 bit per 6F^2) x halved SA area from sharing (~1.5x) = ~9-10x, with no new process layers, only a periphery redesign.

title: Eliminate the DLL and clock tree with delay-insensitive handshake I/O
idea: Replace the DRAM's DLL, clock distribution and read-preamble training with a 4-phase bundled-data handshake per byte lane. The die returns data with a completion strobe generated by a replica bitline that tracks the real array, so it needs no clock at all.
why: Removes the DLL and clock tree (~2-3% of area, 10-15% of always-on I/O power). Power-down exit becomes instant, and latency follows real silicon instead of worst-case guardbands (typical tRCD -10-20%).

title: SiGe bipolar global sense amps on a U.S. BiCMOS chiplet
idea: Reverse the amplifier family: local bitlines pass their signal through one array-side gain transistor onto global bitlines at 8x relaxed pitch, which cross hybrid bonds to SiGe HBT sense amps on a chiplet from a U.S. BiCMOS line (e.g., Vermont); HBT Vbe matching (~1 mV) beats MOS (~10-15 mV), and the milligrams of germanium per wafer can come from U.S. zinc refining.
why: Facts 7 and 1: ~10x lower offset allows 4x longer bitlines (SA count /4) or ~40% smaller Cs, all built domestically.

title: Self-service: refresh bursts double as sense amp offset self-calibration
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: during each refresh burst one sense amp per mat reads an equalized (shorted) bitline pair and the result steps a 4-bit successive-approximation trim register that back-biases or capacitively offsets that amp; over one refresh window every amp re-trims itself, tracking aging and temperature.
why: Facts 1 and 7: effective offset sigma ~3x lower, so cells need ~30% less signal or amps can be minimum-size, and wafer-level trim test time is removed.

title: Clonal-selection retention profiler RTL for commodity DDR5 on FPGA
idea: Like adaptive immunity, an FPGA controller (DRAM Bender-class) 'challenges' rows with stretched refresh and worst-case patterns. Failing rows are clonally expanded into a Bloom-filter list kept at 64 ms, and negative selection re-tests them to purge false positives and catch VRT drift. Everything else refreshes at 256 ms. Three engineers for 24 months plus $80k of boards, ~$900k total, produce licensable controller RTL.
why: Fact 3: ~4x fewer refreshes for >99.9% of rows saves ~70% of refresh energy and most of the 10-20% bandwidth tax, with no DRAM die change.

title: Fruit-grading line: laser-fused refresh classes per mat
idea: Like a fruit packing line that grades every piece into bins, measure each mat's retention at wafer sort and blow two laser fuses that set its refresh multiplier (1x/2x/4x/8x). The on-die refresh counter then skips cycles for long-retention mats.
why: Most mats retain 4-8x longer than the worst one; refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall ~60-70% for two fuses per mat on 1990s laser repair tools.

title: Ba: barium-titanate Pockels modulators replace DRAM DQ SerDes
idea: Bond epitaxial BaTiO3 electro-optic ring modulators at the DRAM periphery edge so each data group modulates light directly from the column data bus at 25-50 Gb/s, eliminating high-swing DQ drivers, termination and most SerDes logic.
why: DDR5 I/O at 10-20 pJ/bit (fact 5) could fall to ~1 pJ/bit and pad area shrinks; barium is abundant (barite).

title: Ba: sol-gel barium titanate decoupling capacitors stacked over pads
idea: Spin-coat and cure sol-gel BaTiO3 (thin-film k ~200-500) MIM decoupling capacitors in top metal over pads and buses, processed in air or N2 with no argon sputtering, replacing the MOS decaps that fill periphery white space.
why: Decaps take several percent of die; moving them up frees ~3-5% area (fact 7).

title: Photovoltaic wordline drivers fed by waveguide light
idea: Inverting 'wordlines are driven by metal and charge pumps': a BEOL waveguide carries light to series photodiode stacks at each floating-body row segment, generating the gate voltage locally when a row's micro-ring is tuned on, so no high-voltage wordline drivers or pumps exist.
why: Eliminates charge pumps and HV driver stripes and isolates rows electrically (helps disturb); speculative on speed and optical power.

title: Sparsity-biased precharge: assume zero, sense only departures
idea: Reverse the neutral mid-rail reference: for AI tensors where most bits are 0, bitlines precharge to the 0 level and a single-ended detector fires only when a cell pulls the bitline up; rows dominated by 1s are stored inverted with a flag bit.
why: Facts 10 and 8: bitline swing and restore energy scale with the fraction of 1s, -50-70% for sparse data; single-ended detector ~half SA area.

title: Rescue rejected DRAM dies behind a strong-ECC buffer controller
idea: Box: existing dies x existing access x existing SA x ECC buffer chip on module x existing substrate x existing fabs. Buy dies that fail JEDEC bins with <=1% bad bits at scrap prices and package them on modules or CXL cards whose buffer chip runs LDPC plus remapping, sold as a new grade.
why: Usable supply rises right away (recapturing yield loss of a few to 10%) with zero new fabs; cost per bit down.

title: Photoconductive-switch probe card multiplexes thousands of test channels optically
idea: Effect: picosecond photoconductive switching in low-temperature-grown GaAs. Build DRAM wafer probe cards whose fan-out uses LT-GaAs photoconductive switch dies closed by an on-card LED/VCSEL array, so a few tester channels are time-multiplexed across thousands of probe pins with optical control instead of relays.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): tester channel count and test capex per bit fall several-fold; a small team integrates via PCB and MEMS-probe vendors.

title: Trim storage on the cell die makes periphery dies generic
idea: Ideal result: the periphery die carries no identity. Store all array-specific trims (redundancy map, reference offsets) in a small ferroelectric block on the cell die instead of periphery e-fuses, so periphery dies are tested generically and can be re-bonded to any array.
why: Enables periphery rebonding and recycling and removes fuse banks from the periphery die (fact 7).

title: Threshold-graded tier select replaces staircase contacts in 3D
idea: Inverting 'each tier of a 3D stack needs its own staircase contact and driver': each tier's select transistor in a stacked capacitorless (floating-body or thyristor) array is given a different threshold voltage by graded work-function gates, so one shared vertical gate line picks the tier by voltage level.
why: Removes staircase etch and per-tier drivers, a major area and process cost of 26+ tier 3D DRAM; breaks the 3D break-even barrier sooner.

title: Differential-GPS reference cells broadcast decay corrections
idea: Borrowed from differential GPS base stations: a few reference cells per mat, written at known levels, are sensed alongside each row to measure how much charge has leaked since refresh at the current temperature, and that correction trims the mat's shared sense reference.
why: Refresh (fact 3): sense amps correctly read half-decayed cells, stretching the refresh interval ~2x with negligible area.

title: Write-first read infers old bit from charge the driver supplies
idea: Flip read and write order: a per-column-group write driver forces the opened cell to '1' while a charge integrator measures how much charge it delivered (~0 for a stored 1, ~Cs*VDD for a stored 0); the result is latched and 0s are written back. Latch-type sense amp and separate restore phase merge into one driver/integrator.
why: Facts 7 and 8: removes the cross-coupled SA and equalizer (~30% of SA strip area); the integrator sees full Cs*VDD rather than a ~100 mV charge-shared swing, so 2-3 fF cells suffice.

title: Resist-free periphery via area-selective deposition, no imported photoresist
idea: Reverse subtractive patterning: periphery contacts and vias are formed by depositing only where wanted, using area-selective deposition with self-assembled inhibitor monolayers from U.S. chemical suppliers and one coarse e-beam template, eliminating several resist-litho-etch loops.
why: Supply chokepoint: advanced photoresist is ~90% Japanese; also removes ~3-5 litho steps from the periphery flow.

title: Room-temperature Coulomb-blockade electrometer reads half-femtofarad cells
idea: Effect: Coulomb blockade. Put one single-electron transistor with a sub-2 nm Si or metal-nanocluster island (charging energy >10 kT) at each local bitline as an electrometer; its drain current swings full scale for a gate-charge change of e/2, so a storage capacitor 10x smaller (~0.5 fF) still gives a readable swing that then drives a conventional latch.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 10x less Cs lets pillar aspect ratio fall from ~70:1 to ~10:1, removing the hardest etch and deposition steps.

title: Boot-calibrated dummy cells cancel each sense amp's offset
idea: At power-up, measure each SA's offset by sweeping a reference on a dummy bitline cell, then write a compensating charge into a per-bitline dummy cell that is charge-shared with the real cell on every read and refreshed with the row.
why: Sense margin (facts 1, 7): 3-4x lower effective offset allows 2x longer bitlines (half the SA stripes, ~8-10% die area) on existing processes.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembly draws sense-amp fins at bitline pitch
idea: Reverse lithography's role: coarse guides from U.S. interference or e-beam litho steer U.S.-made block copolymers to self-assemble the 20-30 nm fins of SA transistors at exactly the bitline pitch, so SAs pitch-match open bitlines without folding.
why: Facts 4 and 7: replaces EUV on SA-pitch layers and keeps 6F2 open-bitline SAs pitch-matched, SA area ~-20%.

title: Ionic drift leaky-integrator per row counts activations for row hammer
idea: Effect: ion migration. Add a sub-50 nm Ag/SiO2 (or Cu/Ta2O5) ionic cell per row, fed by a small tap from the wordline driver; each ACT pulse pushes a fixed ion dose forward while back-diffusion relaxes it with a ~32-64 ms time constant. Conductance thus encodes activations within the refresh window, and crossing a threshold flags the row for neighbor refresh.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): one BEOL device per row replaces SRAM/CAM counter tables of tens of KB per bank, and the natural decay matches the refresh window at no cost.

title: Dithered minimum-size comparator triplets replace large matched sense pairs
idea: Substitute one large, carefully matched sense pair with three minimum-size comparators per bitline pair, each fed an independent small dither offset, followed by a 3-input majority gate before the restore latch fires. Random offsets average instead of being sized away.
why: Periphery area: matching-driven transistor sizing is the main SA area cost; three minimum devices plus majority cost ~40% less area at equal bit-error rate.

title: Curvature: ring-gate annular transistors make edge-free matched sense amp pairs
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: the cross-coupled sense-amp transistors are drawn as annular (ring-gate) devices with the drain in the centre, so there is no STI channel edge; edge-related threshold mismatch and narrow-width effects, a major part of sense-amp offset, disappear, and curvilinear masks from multi-beam writers make the rings printable.
why: Facts 1 and 7: sense-amp offset sigma ~-30-40%, so the latch can be ~30% smaller or the cell signal requirement can drop by ~10 mV.

title: Axon-hillock NbO2 spiking threshold element replacing large matched sense pairs
idea: Like the axon hillock's all-or-nothing spike, a nanoscale NbO2 Mott threshold switch plus series capacitor at each bitline pair forms a relaxation 'neuron'. It fires only when the differential charge passes a programmable bias threshold, turning a few-mV signal into a large spike that sets a minimal latch. Threshold is trimmed by bias, not by big matched transistors.
why: Fact 7: sense-amp input pairs are sized large to beat Vt mismatch. A trimmed spiking element could shrink sense-amp transistor area 3-4x and the sense-amp stripe ~25%.

title: Right-to-repair rule exposing spare rows to operators
idea: Ideal result: owners fix memory themselves. Require DRAM to expose a standard post-package repair command set, spare-row counts and repair logs to the OS, so data centers repair faults in place rather than return modules.
why: Usable supply: fewer discarded modules; a low-cost policy lever during the shortage.

title: Ring-counter time-slot addressing for streaming weight mats
idea: Replace the address with time: mats dedicated to streamed AI weights use a shift-register token that walks the wordlines in fixed order, one per clock, so a row's address is simply its time slot; random access remains only at mat level and row decoders shrink to one token flop per row.
why: Row-decoder area falls ~70-80% in streaming mats (fact 7) and address energy disappears; weight-sweep workloads lose nothing.

title: Vernier decoders address sub-lithographic spacer wires, learned after fab
idea: Failure mined: the HP and Caltech nanowire/molecular crossbars died because nothing could address 5 nm-pitch wires from 50 nm-pitch lithography. Fix: pattern array lines by quadruple spacer pitch-splitting to ~6 nm half-pitch, and cross them with coarse gate lines drawn at a slightly different pitch so each coarse pair coincides over exactly one fine wire, like a vernier scale. A power-up calibration records the actual coincidences in a small remap table.
why: 10x at the same cost: the array reaches ~6 nm half-pitch with zero EUV (spacers are cheap depositions), (12/6)^2 = 4x, times 1.5x for a 4F^2 crosspoint and ~1.7x for decoders that stay at coarse pitch, ~10x bits per cost.

title: Column-periphery zero-skip compression replaces raw data serialization
idea: Substitute raw serialization of the row buffer with zero-run and base-delta compression units in the column periphery that send only non-zero bytes plus a bitmask over the interface. This exploits sparse AI activations and KV caches.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): 1.5-3x fewer bits on the wire for sparse tensors, cutting I/O energy and raising effective bandwidth and capacity.

title: Thermally isolated array tier cooled by microfluidics
idea: Scale-shift the thermal stack: the array wafer bonds to the hot periphery/logic wafer through sparse Cu pillars across a vacuum gap and is cooled from its own backside by microfluidic channels on 10 C rack chilled water, holding cells ~75 C below the logic; with leakage halving every ~10 C, worst-case retention goes from 64 ms to ~10 s and refresh is dropped for step- and token-scoped data.
why: ~150-200x retention deletes refresh (fact 3) and fixes heat-driven retention loss in memory-on-logic stacks.

title: CFET-stacked sense amp transistors to halve SA stripe height
idea: Box: pillar cap x vertical-channel access x CFET-stacked latch x pitch-matched under bitline x bulk Si x sequential 3D integration. The NMOS and PMOS halves of each cross-coupled latch are stacked vertically as complementary FETs, so a full SA fits the bitline pitch of a 4F^2 array.
why: SA stripe height -50%, allowing 4F^2 arrays without SA pitch limits; periphery -10-15% of die.

title: Rod-cell cascade: vertical bipolar preamp at every bitline segment
idea: A rod cell turns one photon into a million-fold cascade from a tiny first stage. Build a vertical n-p-n transistor under each short bitline segment, with the segment driving its floating base, so a few-fC cell dump becomes a 10-30x larger collector current onto a global sense line before any MOS latch.
why: Bipolar current gain lets one global SA serve 4-8 segments and tolerate smaller Cs, roughly halving SA count (facts 1, 7).

title: Run DRAM hot at 105 C without double-rate refresh
idea: Box: standard cap x Si access x temperature-aware soft SA x dense hot packaging x bulk Si x standard. The array may run at 105 C on base refresh; thermally accelerated leakage pushes raw BER up to ~1%, the code absorbs it, and packages can sit closer to accelerators.
why: Energy: removes refresh doubling and some cooling; tighter co-packaging cuts data-movement pJ/bit.

title: Periphery foundry shuttle: the DRAM fab access startups never got
idea: Failure mined: Z-RAM, T-RAM and Nantero each died partly because they could never prove their sensing or cells inside a real DRAM flow. Fix: a for-profit multi-project-wafer service on a U.S. DRAM pilot line that sells 1 mm^2 slots next to a standard array. Startups drop in new sense amps, decoders or cells and get silicon back in 10 weeks.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity: a periphery experiment drops from ~$50M to ~$100k, and learning cycles run ~5x faster.

title: Triple bitline length to 1536 cells, accept 1% signal failures
idea: Box: standard cap x Si access x standard SA x long-bitline mats x bulk Si x standard. Cut the number of SA stripes ~3x by hanging 1536 cells per bitline; the lower transfer ratio leaves ~1% of weak cells unreadable, and the code absorbs them.
why: Periphery: SA stripes -65% (~10% of die area), cost per bit ~-10%.

title: Empty mailbox flag: zero-word detect skips internal data toggling
idea: Don't open the mailbox if it is empty: a wired-NOR at each local sense-amp group flags all-zero 64-bit words, and the chip sends a 1-bit flag on a side line instead of toggling the global data lines, I/O drivers and PHY; ReLU activations, sparse weights and fresh pages are 50-90% zeros.
why: Internal data movement plus I/O is most of access energy; skipping zero words cuts it ~2-10x depending on sparsity, ~10x on sparse AI tensors.

title: Leakage-replica analog refresh timer built from access transistors
idea: Make the refresh clock a capacitor discharged by a bank of access transistors identical to the array's (same doping, GIDL and junction), so its period follows the true leakage physics: ni ~7x up from 85 to 125 C and aging included, without temperature tables.
why: Refresh (fact 3): removes 2-4x worst-case guardband, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss at hot.

title: Lock-in AC tone read buries memristor sneak currents
idea: Failure mined: HP's TiO2 memristor crossbar died on sneak-path currents and line leakage that swamped the selected cell. Fix: put a small 200 MHz tone on the selected wordline only, hold all other lines at AC ground, and read the bitline through a mixer and integrator locked to that tone. DC bias leakage, half-select currents and 1/f noise all fall outside the detection band.
why: Selectorless 1k x 1k tiles can be read with >30 dB rejection of the background. That removes selector layers and makes tiles 4-16x larger, so decoders and sense amps take a smaller share of die area.

title: Skipping: read-once scratch memory omits restore and refresh circuits
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping: for streaming activations and KV-cache spills written once and read once within milliseconds, the cell is read destructively and restore and refresh are skipped entirely; the periphery loses write-back drivers, refresh counters and the restore VPP budget, and cells need only ~5 ms retention, so a ~0.5 fF planar capacitor is enough.
why: 100x path: no high-aspect-ratio capacitor, periphery ~30% smaller and BEOL-stackable planar cells on mature nodes; trade-offs: each datum is consumed by its read (re-reads need a host copy) and data expires after milliseconds. Attacks Facts 1, 3 and 8.

title: Core-memory coincident selection from one shield-strip cut mask
idea: Core memory switched only the bit where X and Y half-currents coincided. One added cut mask splits the inter-channel shield (back-gate) plate of a vertical-channel array into strips that run along the bitline direction, one strip per 1/16 of a row. A cell turns on only when its row wordline and its segment strip are both raised, and each alone is subthreshold.
why: Only the addressed 1/16 of a row dumps charge and is sensed, cutting the 128x overfetch to ~8x (fact 8) and activation energy ~10x, and it shrinks the row-hammer blast radius (fact 9).

title: Gecko-setae microfiber probe card contacting every die at once
idea: Gecko feet make reliable contact through millions of compliant setae. A probe card made of conductive CNT-cored polymer micro-pillars, molded from a reusable silicon master, touches every die on a 300 mm wafer at once with gentle self-conforming force. On-die BIST means each die needs only power plus a serial line. University-cleanroom molding and prototype, ~$900k in 24 months.
why: Capital/test: one touchdown per wafer with cheap replicated cards could cut test cost per bit 30-50% and free tester capex.

title: Same capacitor, +58% bits: tri-level cells with stepped-reference sensing
idea: Limit: no new cell and no new litho, only periphery. Store three charge levels (0, 1/2, 1) and sense in two steps: first against a +1/3 reference, then against a -1/3 reference created by coupling a small trim capacitor, packing 3 bits into 2 cells.
why: Density and cost per bit: +58% bits from the same array, paid for by ~20% more SA area and tighter margins, so it works best paired with offset trimming.

title: Complementary MTJ voltage divider readable by an inverter
idea: Inverting 'MRAM needs a sensitive sense amp': each bit is two MTJs written to opposite states and stacked as a voltage divider, so the mid-node swings ~0.3 V between states and a plain skewed inverter at the column replaces the current-mode sense amp.
why: Removes reference cells and analog sense amps, cutting column periphery ~25% and read latency to a few ns; capacitor-free.

title: MTJ-shadowed sense latches give a nonvolatile row buffer
idea: Substitute the purely volatile sense latch with a latch shadowed by a pair of MTJs written on precharge. Periphery can then be hard power-gated between bursts, and open rows reload from the MTJs in nanoseconds without reactivating the array.
why: Idle energy: periphery leakage dominates idle power at advanced nodes; power-gating plus instant row-buffer recall cuts idle power by ~30-50% and avoids re-activate energy.

title: Widrow memistor trims sense-amp offset in one via
idea: Revive Widrow's 1960 memistor, a three-terminal electroplated resistor. One added via mask fills a Cu/GeSe electrolyte plug in each sense amp's tail leg, which is plated up or down at test (and retouched in the field) to null that amp's measured Vt offset.
why: With offset trimmed out, sense transistors can shrink to near minimum size because mismatch no longer sets W·L: ~2-3x smaller sense stripes (fact 7) and ~40% less required signal (fact 1).

title: Nano-vacuum-channel field-emission wordline drivers
idea: Electrons crossing a ~50 nm vacuum gap by field emission have no oxide to break down, no BTI, and no junction leakage; such switches tolerate far beyond 125 C. Use them as high-voltage wordline/plate switches fabricated in BEOL cavities.
why: Removes TDDB and BTI limits on 3 V drivers (fact 10) and moves drivers off silicon (fact 7).

title: Po: biased sense amps that favor the decaying state
idea: Po: a sense amp that is deliberately unfair. Because only the charged state leaks (true cells toward '0', anti cells toward '1'), give every SA a designed offset (asymmetric device sizing or a shifted bitline precharge) toward the leaky state, with the skew direction flipped per mat to match true/anti-cell layout in open-bitline arrays.
why: Refresh (#3): the full-swing non-leaking state has margin to spare, so lending it to the decaying state extends the retention tail ~1.5-2x, cutting refresh energy (46 fJ/bit) and bandwidth loss proportionally.

title: District-heating supply of wordline high voltage from base die
idea: Like a district heating plant replacing a boiler in every house, generate VPP (~3 V) and negative back-bias in one efficient inductive or switched-capacitor converter on the HBM base die or DIMM PMIC, and deliver them to every core die through dedicated TSVs/pads instead of many small on-die charge pumps.
why: Periphery area (~5-7% of die in pumps and pump caps) and energy: pump efficiency rises from ~30% to ~85%, halving wordline supply energy.

title: Open sense-interface standard makes periphery dies universal and reusable
idea: Ideal result: any cell array plugs into any periphery. Define a bond-level standard (bitline pitch, timing, trim protocol) between cell dies and periphery dies, so U.S.-made periphery dies work with multiple cell fabs and can be re-bonded to the next array generation.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: periphery made on mature U.S. nodes, cell dies dual-sourced, periphery reusable across generations.

title: Charge-redistribution SAR sensing stores three levels per cell
idea: Worse: spend all margin storing a single bit per cell. Flip: share the bitline charge onto binary-weighted reference capacitors in a two-step successive-approximation sense amp that resolves three charge levels (1.58 bits/cell), Gray-coded so a one-level slip becomes a single-bit ECC-correctable error.
why: Density and cost per bit: ~58% more bits per cell area if the signal margin holds.

title: Progressive-die cascade: three charge-transfer stages pre-amplify before latching
idea: Like a progressive stamping die that forms a part through several small stations, pass the bitline charge through three cascaded switched-capacitor charge-transfer stages, each dumping charge from a larger capacitor onto one ~3x smaller. The result is ~20-27x voltage gain before a relaxed latch fires.
why: A large signal at the latch tolerates small, high-offset SA devices (SA area ~-40%) and lets bitlines carry 2-3x more cells, or allows Cs to fall ~2x toward 2-3 fF.

title: Latching vertical-thyristor sub-wordline drivers from Kilopass VLT
idea: Failure mined: Kilopass's vertical layered thyristor (VLT) DRAM was abandoned over cell variability and the lack of a fab partner. Fix: use the VLT device where variability is harmless, as the sub-wordline driver. One anode pulse latches it on to drive the 3 V wordline and a cathode pull resets it, so each driver is a single ~4F^2 vertical device with no static decoder hold state.
why: Sub-wordline driver and local decoder strips are ~8-10% of the die. A vertical latching driver cuts them ~3x and removes static hold power, giving back ~5-6% of die area.

title: Bucket-brigade row buffer replaces column decoder and datalines
idea: Turn the sensed row into a CCD-style charge-transfer shift register: after sensing, bits march out of the stripe edge in parallel lanes at GHz rates straight into the serializer, so the column decoder, column-select lines and global I/O sense amps are gone. This combines CCD readout with the DRAM row buffer.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and overfetch (fact 8): the column path is ~10% of die; streaming full rows turns the 128x overfetch into useful data for AI/streaming, ~3-5x lower pJ per useful bit.

title: Time-domain bitline sensing with shared TDCs on bonded logic wafer
idea: Box: pillar 1T1C x buried-channel access x time-domain sensing x CMOS-under-array x bulk Si x 28 nm logic wafer bonded. Each bitline's post-charge-share voltage starves a tiny inverter so the bit becomes a delay, and one time-to-digital converter serves 16 bitlines through a delay-line race, replacing 16 latch SAs with 16 inverters plus 1 TDC.
why: Periphery (~49% of die): SA stripe area -50-60%; time-domain gain stays cheap at low voltage, easing the voltage floor.

title: Noise as resource: dithered majority-vote sensing with tiny comparators
idea: Limit: comparator offset (sigma ~20 mV) is bigger than the signal (~15 mV). Inject a calibrated random dither on the reference, fire a minimum-size, unmatched, non-loading comparator 7-15 times in ~3 ns, and count: the signal skews the probability of ones (stochastic resonance), so the majority recovers the bit, and only then does the restore driver fire.
why: Sense margin and periphery area: comparators 4x smaller, plus tolerance of smaller Cs or longer bitlines (facts 1, 7).

title: 3D DRAM staircase rebuilt as the wordline-driver farm
idea: Rearrange the dead staircase of stacked 3D DRAM: each step landing hosts vertical-channel transistors grown in the same deposition steps as the tiers, acting as tier-select and local wordline drivers, so the contact region becomes active periphery.
why: Facts 2 and 7: the staircase is ~10-15% of 3D array area; reusing it as drivers shrinks the CMOS needed under the array and the contact count routed to it.

title: Tweezers: 64-cell micro-row activation ends page overfetch
idea: Pick one item with tweezers instead of scooping the tray: split each wordline into 64-cell micro-rows with a 2-transistor local AND driver (global wordline x column-group select), so an access opens and senses only the 64-512 cells requested, not an 8 kb page.
why: Destructive read with 128x overfetch (fact 8, ~5.9 pJ per useful bit): sensing energy per useful bit falls ~16-100x, so total access energy drops >10x; costs ~5-8% array area for local drivers.

title: Coincident row-and-column-group selection borrowed from core memory
idea: Substitute single-wordline activation with core-memory coincident selection: the access transistor is dual-gated, with the top gate on the row line and a buried back gate on a column-group line, and it conducts only when both are high. Only a 512-bit segment of the row opens.
why: Destructive-read overfetch (fact 8): activated bits drop from ~8K to 512, cutting energy per useful bit up to ~16x on random access, and less charge disturbance also eases row hammer.

title: Coincident row-and-column select with dual-gate access transistors
idea: Inverting 'the wordline alone opens a cell': each access transistor gets a back gate tied to a column-group select line so a cell conducts only where the wordline and its column-group line are both high (like core memory's X-Y coincidence), so an activate opens 64-512 bits instead of 8 KB.
why: Cuts the 128x page overfetch toward 2-8x, lowering random-read energy ~5x from ~5.9 pJ per useful bit, and shrinks the set of rows a hammering pattern can disturb.

title: Po: sense amps take turns — 1:8 charge-parked sensing
idea: Po: a bank with one-eighth of its sense amps. After activation, isolation gates park each bitline's charge-shared signal on the bitline itself; one SA serves 8 bitlines through a mux, sensing and writing back group by group in ~2 ns slots, with the requested column group always sensed first.
why: Periphery (#7): SA+equalizer strips (~15-20% of die) shrink ~7/8, ~10% better cost per bit; first-access tRCD unchanged, only tRAS grows. Parked charge decays over microseconds, so the 16 ns window is safe.

title: Po: never open a full row — column-gated sub-wordlines
idea: Po: a row that is never fully opened. Merge ACT and RD into one command carrying row and column address, and AND the column-group select into each sub-wordline driver so only the ~1 kb segment containing the requested line is activated and sensed.
why: Overfetch (#8): 128x overfetch falls to ~16x for random access, ~5x lower activate energy per useful bit; fewer opened cells also cut aggressor activity (row hammer #9).

title: Ring-oscillator time-domain sensing at 0.4 V array voltage
idea: Energy-harvesting IoT tags have no voltage headroom, so they sense in time: the bitline voltage starves a tiny ring oscillator per column group, and a counter compares its edge count over a fixed window against a reference column. It works at VARY ~0.4 V, where latch SAs fail.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): bitline CV^2 energy down ~5-6x versus a 1 V VARY; a digital SA scales with logic nodes.

title: Storage-node-controlled ring-oscillator readout stores two bits per gain cell
idea: Effect: voltage-controlled oscillation frequency. In a 2T gain cell, the storage node gates the current source of a short current-starved ring oscillator shared per column group; a read counts oscillations for ~10 ns, so four charge levels map to clearly separated counts. The count is digital and immune to bitline offset.
why: Density/cost per bit: 2 bits per cell doubles gain-cell macro density on mature U.S. nodes, and counters replace analog SAs; MPW-feasible.

title: Coin-counting machine: multi-row charge summation read by bitline ADC
idea: A coin counter weighs the pile instead of counting coins one at a time: activate up to 8 rows of a bit-plane at once so their cell charges sum on each bitline, then digitize the analog sum with a 3-bit SAR built from the SA's reference caps, returning popcounts or dot-product partial sums rather than raw bits.
why: One activation replaces 8 activations plus 8x data transfer for reductions and binary/ternary dot products; ~10-30x less energy per useful operation; risks are cell variation and destroyed data needing copy rows.

title: Quarter-size sense amps with one-time digital offset trim
idea: MINIFY SA transistors 4x and accept ~40 mV offset; at wafer test, measure each SA's offset and store a 4-bit code in a dense trim array that drives a small capacitive DAC on the latch node during every sense.
why: Fact 7: SA area -50% while effective offset returns to <5 mV, which in turn tolerates smaller Cs (Fact 1).

title: LIDAR time-to-digital converter turns bitline voltage into delay
idea: Borrowed from automotive LIDAR TDCs: the bitline voltage starves a short inverter chain so a 20 mV difference becomes ~30 ps of delay, and a digitally calibrated arbiter flip-flop decides the bit from arrival order. No large matched cross-coupled latch is needed.
why: Periphery area and voltage floor (facts 7, 10): sense-amp area down ~2x and sensing at 0.6 V, since time-domain resolution does not shrink with supply.

title: Room-temperature single-electron electrometers read 300-electron cells
idea: MINIFY the stored charge 100x: sub-2 nm metal or Si-nanocrystal single-electron transistors gate-coupled to short local bitlines sense ~50 aC (about 300 electrons), so the storage capacitor shrinks to ~0.05 fF and the tall pillar disappears.
why: Facts 1-2: eliminates the capacitor wall and enables thin planar 3D tiers, potentially 3-5x density; room-temperature SET uniformity is unproven.

title: Tape-style run-length coding lets bitlines pack tighter
idea: Magnetic tape used run-length-limited codes to avoid worst-case flux patterns. Add a 64b/68b write encoder that forbids the worst bitline coupling patterns, such as a lone 1 between 0s on adjacent bitlines of one row, so sense amps never see the worst aggressor sums. No mask is added at all.
why: Worst-case coupling noise drops ~40%, allowing ~20-25% tighter bitline pitch or less margin (facts 1, 4) for 6% capacity overhead.

title: Eliminate the dual gate oxide with drain-extended cascode wordline drivers
idea: Build every 3 V wordline-driver device as a thin-oxide drain-extended or two-high cascode transistor, so one gate oxidation serves the whole die. This removes the thick-oxide mask and its HF strip; pre-gate cleans use SC1/SC2 plus an in-situ H2 bake instead of HF-last.
why: Removes one mask, the HF strip and a gate-stack variant from the periphery (fact 7), at a ~10% area cost in drivers.

title: DWDM wavelength-addressed wordlines through transparent glass
idea: Borrowed from telecom DWDM: each wordline driver on a glass panel is a photo-TFT under a thin-film Fabry-Perot filter tuned to one of 64 wavelengths, and a fast tunable laser beneath the transparent substrate selects a row by color, with 1-of-16 electrical predecode choosing the mat.
why: Periphery: optical selection replaces row decoders and global address wiring, cutting decoder area ~70% in exchange for an off-panel photonic source.

title: Selectron binary-stripe decoders coded by one depletion implant
idea: RCA's 1946 Selectron picked one of 256 spots with crossed bars driven by binary address pairs. Build each row decoder as a pitch-matched series chain of array-style transistors under true/complement address stripes. The single added depletion-implant mask makes chosen transistors always-on, so the implant pattern alone encodes each row's address.
why: Row decoders at array pitch built from array transistors are ~3x smaller (fact 7), with one non-critical implant mask and no EUV (fact 4).

title: Module PMIC supplies wordline high voltage, deleting on-die charge pumps
idea: Worse: generate the 3 V wordline rail and negative back-bias on every die with ~30%-efficient charge pumps. Flip: supply VPP and VBB from GaN or switched-capacitor converters on the module PMIC through dedicated bumps and package planes, deleting on-die pumps and their reservoir capacitors.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and voltage-floor energy (fact 10): frees ~4-6% of die and lifts VPP efficiency from ~30% to ~85%.

title: Roaming sense amp sweeps sixteen bitlines inside their charge-hold window
idea: Reverse the one-amp-per-bitline layout: after charge sharing, a bitline holds its ~100 mV signal for ~1-2 us, so one offset-cancelled sense amp steps through a 16:1 mux, regenerating and restoring each bitline in turn, requested column first. The data waits for the amp instead of each amp waiting for data.
why: Periphery (fact 7): bitline SA area falls ~8-16x, returning ~10-15% of the die to cells; first-column latency unchanged, full-row restore ~16 x 3 ns hidden behind the burst.

title: Stethoscope on a whole mat: aggregate leakage sets refresh
idea: A doctor listens to the whole chest, not one cell. A dedicated idle sentinel mat ties millions of storage junctions to an integrating amplifier that measures aggregate leakage (nA scale) in real time, and the refresh interval tracks that measured leakage rather than worst-case temperature tables.
why: Most hours run far from the worst corner; measured-leakage refresh cuts refresh 2-4x in typical operation, part of the 16-33% idle power (fact 3).

title: Kiln witness cones: in-array cells integrate activation heat-work for row hammer
idea: Like pyrometric cones that slump after enough cumulative kiln heat, each row has a witness cell that gets a small charge kick through a weak device on every activation and leaks it away over time. Refresh reads the witness column and schedules neighbor refresh wherever a witness has slumped past threshold.
why: Replaces megabits of SRAM row-hammer counters in periphery with ~0.1% extra array cells; analog decay tracks hammer physics at ~1k-activation thresholds.

title: Eliminate per-bitline latches: shared time-to-digital bitline sensing
idea: Remove the cross-coupled latch from every bitline pair. After charge sharing, each bitline gates a single discharge transistor onto a shared ramp, and one time-to-digital converter, time-interleaved over 32 bitlines in about 4 ns, records which bitlines cross threshold first. A global restore bus then rewrites the cells through one-transistor restore switches.
why: Periphery (fact 7): SA stripes are ~10-15% of the die; replacing 6-8 matched transistors per pair with 2 small devices cuts SA area ~50-60% (die -5-8%). Costs +2-4 ns latency.

title: Photomultiplier dynodes: electron-multiplying gain register on every bitline
idea: Forced connection to a photomultiplier/EMCCD dynode chain: between cell and sense amp insert a short serial register of 8-10 high-field transfer gates in the SA strip, each adding ~1.2x impact-ionization gain, so a 1 fF cell's ~3,000 signal electrons arrive at the latch as ~15,000-20,000. The register is clocked only during the sense phase.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 5-6x pre-latch gain lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~1 fF, cutting pillar AR from ~70:1 toward ~20:1 or making small-cap 3D tiers viable; risks are excess gain noise and the high clock voltage.

title: Library whisper: virtual-ground charge-transfer sensing keeps bitlines frozen
idea: In a library nobody raises their voice: hold every bitline at a fixed potential with a cascode charge-transfer amplifier so it never swings; the cell's charge flows through into a ~0.5 fF integrating node at the SA, giving a large local voltage, and restore pushes the same charge back through the cascode.
why: The ~100 fF bitline never charges or discharges, so bitline CV2, the dominant activation term, disappears; only cell charge moves, ~10-20x less array energy; risk is cascode speed and offset at 24 nm pitch.

title: Camcorder-CCD row buffer: charge packets shuffle to few amplifiers
idea: Borrow the 1990s CCD imager: on activate, every bitline's charge is dumped into a buried-channel CCD register under the SA strip, which holds the row in the charge domain. Only the requested columns are clocked a few stages to floating-diffusion amplifiers with correlated double sampling, then the packets are shifted back to restore.
why: One low-noise amplifier per 8-16 columns instead of one SA per column (SA area -80%); correlated double sampling resolves ~1,000-electron packets, so tiny planar capacitors made at 180 nm can be read.

title: Beforehand cushioning: weak-written sentinel rows trigger early mat refresh
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: each mat reserves two sentinel rows that are written at only ~70% of the array voltage, making them deliberately weaker than any data row; they are read on every refresh pass, and the first sentinel failure raises that mat's refresh rate before real data is at risk.
why: Fact 3: lets the default refresh interval be set aggressively (~2x longer) with a built-in early warning, so ~30-40% of refresh energy is saved without per-die retention testing.

title: Periphery evicted upstairs: oxide-tellurium CMOS sense amps over array
idea: Within a 400 C budget, build sense amps and decoders in BEOL tiers directly above the cell array using n-type IGZO (deposited ~300 C) and p-type tellurium TFTs (evaporated near room temperature), MINIFYING periphery footprint on silicon toward zero.
why: Fact 7: periphery share of die from ~49% to ~15%, ~1.6x bits per wafer; tellurium p-FET stability is the main risk.

title: Dendritic-tree row decoders in BEOL oxide transistors over the mats
idea: Dendrites compute at branch points, so build the row predecode/decode as a binary tree of 2-input coincidence (AND) gates made from IGZO or poly-Si TFTs in the BEOL directly above the cell mats. Pipelining hides TFT slowness. Only the final high-voltage wordline drivers stay in the silicon strip.
why: Fact 7: decoder strips are ~10-15% of the die. Moving the logic part into otherwise empty BEOL volume could shrink the die ~8-12% without hybrid-bonding capex.

title: Complementary nanotube sense amps built directly over the array
idea: Inverting 'sense amps must sit in the silicon substrate': cross-coupled sense amps are fabricated from complementary carbon-nanotube FETs at <400 C in the BEOL directly above the cell mats, pitch-matched to the bitlines through short vias.
why: Moves the largest periphery block off the substrate, shrinking the die ~20-25%; the low-temperature process does not damage capacitors below.

title: Lunar-fab materials: molybdenum periphery contacts and helium-free processing
idea: Design periphery for a fab with no tungsten or helium, as on a Moon base: periphery contact plugs and wordline straps use ALD molybdenum or ruthenium instead of W/WF6, and wafer backside cooling uses hydrogen-argon blends instead of helium, all at DUV rules.
why: Removes chokepoints (tungsten ~80% China, Qatari helium offline) from periphery and lowers small-via resistance.

title: Drip-irrigation valves: column-gated local wordlines stop overfetch
idea: Like drip lines watering only the plants that need it, split each 8 kb row into 32 segments whose local wordline is gated by a BEOL vertical select transistor driven from the column address, so an activate opens only the 256 bits being read.
why: Overfetch/destructive read (~5.9 pJ per useful bit, 128x overfetch): random-access activate energy falls ~10-20x, and row-hammer exposure falls too.

title: HDD PRML joint detection replaces bitline shielding and twisting
idea: Treat bitline-to-bitline coupling as intersymbol interference, as an HDD read channel does: sample 8 adjacent bitlines with two-level comparators, run a 4-state Viterbi detector in the column path that decides all 8 jointly, then restore. Shield lines, twist regions and folded layouts are dropped for minimum-pitch open bitlines.
why: Periphery/density: removes twist and shield overhead (~5-8% of array plus SA stripe) and tolerates 2x coupling, making 4F2 open-bitline cells viable without a noise penalty.

title: Dirty-row trickle persistence bounds the power-fail energy budget
idea: Constraint: survive sudden power loss with only a tiny hold-up capacitor. Periphery keeps one dirty bit per row and an in-die copy engine uses idle refresh slots to copy dirty rows into an on-die NV bank, capping outstanding dirty rows at N (e.g., 4k), so hold-up energy covers just N rows.
why: Backup energy and capacitor size drop 100-1000x compared with a full-die dump; the copy reuses refresh bandwidth that is spent anyway (fact 3).

title: Po: a chip sold on its periodic table — abundance preference
idea: Po: a memory chip graded by its periodic table. Federal procurement and CHIPS rules give DRAM whose periphery and interconnect use only Earth-abundant elements (certified BOM: no W, Co, Ru, Ta, Hf, In, Ga) a 10% purchase preference and accelerated depreciation on the tooling.
why: Scarce resources and U.S. manufacturability: a demand signal that pays for the periphery material changes and insulates supply from tungsten and gallium export controls.

title: Hybrid-bonded GaN HEMT tier for wordline drivers and pumps
idea: GaN, used in space and 200 C power electronics, has ~10x silicon's breakdown field; a thin GaN-on-Si e-mode HEMT tier hybrid-bonded under the array hosts sub-wordline drivers and VPP switches, delivering 3-4 V swings with tiny high-voltage devices instead of thick-oxide silicon.
why: SWD and high-voltage periphery (~10-15% of die) shrink ~3x; higher wordline overdrive and deeper negative wordline cut the leakage tail (fact 3).

title: Size sense amps for 3.5 sigma, repair the tail by columns
idea: Time-shift the design decision to wafer test: SA input pairs are sized for 3.5-sigma Pelgrom offset instead of ~6 sigma, and the ~0.02% of SAs whose offset fails at sort are mapped out once, for the chip's years-long life, with extra spare columns.
why: Matching-device area scales with the square of the sigma target, so SA input pairs shrink ~3x, SA stripes ~25-35%, about 5-8% of die area (fact 7).

title: Leakier canary cells invalidate rows of a clean DRAM cache
idea: Time-shift retention into a cache lifetime: each row has a deliberately leakier canary cell (narrower storage node, ~5x faster decay), DRAM serves only as a clean cache over flash or NV holding inference weights, and when a read finds the canary drained the row is treated as a miss and refetched, never refreshed.
why: Deletes refresh (fact 3) and the refresh-engine periphery (fact 7); refetches stay <1% of traffic when weights are read every few seconds.
